verdicts.reason: Citing a named real incident as direct evidence is not the same as building an analogy to a comparator program and extracting a transferable lesson.
Proposing measurement and feedback machinery is distinct from analyzing how the rule fails under unusual conditions.
Spotting an internal conflation of sub-cases is unrelated to comparing the rule against other identified rules or dockets.
X requires load-bearing quantities (own operational numbers qualify) while Y requires an external primary source that may contain no numbers at all.
A comment can supply precise replacement parameters without ever identifying the specific provision they would replace, which Y demands.
Both score a step-by-step causal trace from the proposal to concrete effects, with identical zero anchors of bare assertion.
Rebutting an objection to one's own position is a different act from supplying a substitute approach to the agency's goal.
Y credits any exact actionable request (e.g., a deadline change) while X requires an alternative plus its causal mechanism.
X requires the traced outcome to be perverse relative to the rule's stated purpose; Y credits any specified multi-step chain.
Pinpointing proposed provisions and explaining their operation differs from applying governing statutory or precedential language.
Both measure a specified multi-step causal chain from rule to outcome versus unconnected assertion.
Countering the agency's stated rationale is different from adding facts the record does not yet contain.
Laying out how the proposal itself would be executed differs from proposing a substitute design that preserves the objective.
Proposing prospective data collection is distinct from presenting and interpreting numbers already in hand.
X credits depth of operational understanding from any source including professional expertise, while Y requires the commenter's own first-hand performance of the activity.
Designing forward-looking monitoring is not the same as quantifying present effects against a baseline.
Weighing competing objectives and justifying a balance is distinct from supplying a concrete alternative.
X additionally requires the experience be tied to a cited provision, which a purely operational first-hand account need not do.
Both score identification of specific affected groups plus the mechanism of asymmetric cost/benefit exposure, penalizing undifferentiated 'the public'.
Both reward a specific implementable alternative to an opposed provision with an account of why it serves the agency's goal; the mechanism wording is a stylistic difference.
Correcting an error in the proposal's wording is not the same as specifying an exact requested change.
Both score whether legal conclusions are grounded in statutory, regulatory, or precedential text applied to the proposal.
Both require first-person experience tightly bound to a specific provision or mechanism, and both zero out unanchored personal narrative.
X demands the strongest contrary rationale stated accurately and answered on its terms; Y is satisfied by rebutting any one specific objection, including a weak one.
Identifying barriers to implementation is the critical mirror of constructing a workable pathway; supportive comments can score high on Y and zero on X.
Both score naming other specific legal instruments and reasoning about consistency or tension with the proposal.
Equity incidence across populations is distinct from whether the approach misfires in materially different operating contexts.
Both measure identified interactions, conflicts, or redundancy across related rules and systems versus treating the proposal in isolation.
A future systemic risk can be flagged without pointing to any textual scenario the rule fails to cover, which Y requires.
Both score analysis of timing, sequencing, seasonality, and phase-in connected to the rule's effects.
A developed ultra-vires argument and the mere presence of part/section CFR citations are almost independent features.
Targeting a proposed provision with a revision differs from invoking and applying governing external legal text.
Both operationalize the same thing: a multi-step chain with each link's mechanism named, versus a single-step assertion.
Calibrated partial agreement measures how the comment separates endorsement from objection, not whether it targets rule text with a revision.
X specifically requires two rival readings with divergent consequences; Y credits any identified error or misstatement in the quoted text.
Proposing a better alternative is not the same as explaining who must act and how the transition to the proposal itself would occur.
Rule-specific numeric content is distinct from the precision of the change being requested.
Steelmanning and answering the best contrary argument differs from explicitly comparing competing objectives and defending a balance.
Offering a substitute design and proposing measurement/verification machinery are separate contributions.
Supplying an alternative design is distinct from acknowledging and weighing opposing considerations.
Both require an implementable alternative accompanied by a rationale for why it works while preserving the agency's objective.
Adding new facts to the record is nearly the opposite of arguing from the agency's own preamble material.
Both score concrete first-hand or local observation translated into a generalizable, rule-relevant implication.
Tracing consequences of the proposal differs from proposing an alternative to it.
An internal conflation of categories is unrelated to conflicts or duplication across other rules and agencies.
Pinpointing a provision and requesting a revision differs from grounding the proposal in delegated authority and legal limits.
A missed internal distinction is a different defect from an identified inconsistency with a named external instrument.
Explaining how the rule causes harm is distinct from proposing and justifying a substitute rule.
Both score whether the comment identifies the governing legal provision and reasons from its text to the proposal rather than asserting a conclusion.
Self-containment penalizes reliance on external material, whereas Y rewards citing external sources; they can even move in opposite directions.
Presenting interpreted data now is different from proposing indicators and verification going forward.
Y is a composite additionally requiring the fact be first-hand and paired with an explicit decision consequence, neither of which X demands.
X credits any concrete multi-step spillover chain; Y requires the outcome to be diametrically opposed to the rule's stated purpose.
Targeting rule text with a revision is unrelated to exposing sub-cases the rule wrongly treats alike.
Naming what the proposal omits is the complement of engaging and revising what the proposal does say.
X centers foreseeable failure conditions and safeguards; Y centers heterogeneity of contexts and populations, and a comment can do one without the other.
Diagnosing implementation barriers is distinct from proposing a mechanism-backed alternative.
Y requires engaging the agency's own NPRM reasoning specifically, while X credits response to any opposing consideration.
Both score whether the requested action is precise enough for a drafter to act on versus a vague directional preference.
An uncovered scenario in the rule's own text is different from a consistency comparison against another identified rule.
Offering an alternative is distinct from stating and answering the strongest contrary rationale.
A comment can pinpoint a provision and request a revision without alleging any error, ambiguity, or misstatement in its wording.
Both score epistemic calibration: separating established fact from inference and assumption and being explicit about uncertainty.
Both reward exact replacement text, thresholds, or defined procedures and zero out generic support or opposition.
X engages the operative rule text's wording; Y engages the preamble's rationale, cost figures, and cited studies.
Y additionally requires the traced outcome to invert the rule's stated purpose, which a plain mechanism chain need not do.
Both require numbers that are bound to the rule's operation and do interpretive work rather than sitting as decoration.
A comment can weigh policy costs and benefits without ever acknowledging an objection to its own position, and vice versa.
Arguing perverse effects of the rule is distinct from proposing a workable substitute.
Rule-specific numeric content is unrelated to cross-referencing other rules or dockets.
Anticipating a future unaddressed problem differs from supplying a documented instance that falsifies a premise the rule rests on.
Y is broader, covering undelivered commitments and unassigned responsibilities that involve no textual scenario ambiguity at all.
X credits neutral description of actors, workflows, and dependencies, while Y requires a named actor who is unprepared plus an operational consequence.
X keys on the causal mechanism of the alternative, Y on whether its operative parameters are filled in; a threshold with no rationale splits them.
Both score a concrete linked sequence from proposal through behavior to downstream consequences versus a single-step claim.
Pinpointing text in this proposal is unrelated to identifying cross-rule interactions and duplication.
Both require a specific, checkable real-world instance that contradicts a premise the proposal depends on.
Naming a specific place or facility is not the same as tracing differential winners and losers across groups.
Both score the commenter's own derived monetary compliance-cost figures with a stated basis.
Supplying provision-linked numbers is distinct from identifying a provision and specifying a revision.
Both score a concrete step-by-step causal trace from the requirement to specific effects.
Both require specific numbers that actively support the argument about the provision rather than serving as decoration.
Both score whether the requested change is exact and drafter-actionable versus a bare position statement.
Correcting the proposal's own wording is unrelated to comparing it against another identified rule or docket.
Y additionally requires traceable sourcing of the quantities, so well-integrated but unsourced numbers score high on X and mid on Y.
Constructing an implementation pathway is the constructive counterpart of identifying an unprepared actor and a resulting gap.
Both score identification of specific practical implementation deficits — missing systems, unprepared actors — and the reason they matter.
Both score whether a legal argument identifies the right provision and reasons from it, rather than asserting a conclusion or bare citation.
Both score proposals for measurable data collection, testing, monitoring, and validation tied to the decision.
Both require naming a particular other legal instrument and reasoning about its consistency with the proposal.
Y specifically requires comparison to a baseline or historical level, which integrated quantitative argument need not include.
Both score an implementable alternative that still achieves the agency's underlying objective, offered in place of pure rejection.
X requires a perverse, purpose-inverting outcome; Y credits any credible mechanism to concrete effects, including intended ones.
Distributional asymmetry across groups is a different axis from geographic or institutional localization of an impact.
Y requires the named instance to cut against the agency's stated premise, while X credits any named real instance offered as evidence.
Both score identification of distinct affected populations with the mechanism of their unequal exposure to costs and benefits.
Cross-system and jurisdictional spillovers are a different dimension from effects unfolding over time.
Attacking a definition or category boundary differs from describing a concrete scenario the text leaves unresolved.
A missing commitment or unanswered question in the proposal need involve no unprepared actor or operational capacity gap.
Y additionally requires the experience to surface a factual dynamic the agency appears unaware of, beyond reporting first-hand operational detail.
Argument density across the whole comment is unrelated to the rigor of a legal argument.
Both score explicit comparison of competing benefits, costs, and affected parties versus one-sided advocacy.
Handling tradeoffs is unrelated to focus, ranking of recommendations, and decision-readiness.
Prioritization and focus are unrelated to identifying an unanticipated future problem.
Both require a specific step-by-step causal chain with each mechanism named rather than a bare assertion of harm.
Both score named groups plus the mechanism of their differential gain or loss, zeroing out generic 'stakeholders'.
Self-containment is about dependence on external attachments; density is about the background-to-argument ratio within the text.
Both turn on whether the comment engages opposing considerations at all, and their zero anchors of one-sided advocacy are effectively identical.
X requires anchoring to a cited provision, while Y requires revealing a dynamic the agency has missed; either can appear without the other.
Both score identification of specific populations bearing distinct costs or benefits with the allocation mechanism explained.
Rebutting an external objection is not the same as conceding a genuine limitation of one's own position.
The precision of a request is unrelated to whether the comment surfaces an unanticipated future problem.
Proposing a mechanism-backed alternative is distinct from tracing the proposed rule's own causal consequences.
Near-verbatim restatements: claims supported by identifiable studies, records, or measurements relevant to the proposal.
An implementation capacity gap is one narrow species of unanticipated problem; most forward-looking risks involve no actor-readiness analysis.
X rewards laying out a workable path with transition and timing, while Y rewards operational workflow detail showing where the proposal breaks.
Y credits any behavioral-response causal chain; X requires the result to be diametrically opposed to the rule's purpose.
Both score a specified multi-step causal sequence from the proposal to concrete consequences.
First-hand operational description and emotional intensity are essentially orthogonal, often inversely related.
Y requires diagnosing a structural design flaw in addition to the alternative, which X does not ask for at all.
X credits neutral description of actors, workflows, and dependencies, while Y requires identified barriers that block implementation.
Naming a provision and requesting a revision is different from exposing a scenario the text fails to resolve.
An uncovered scenario is a gap in coverage; a conflated distinction is over-broad uniform treatment of unlike cases.
Y requires drafting-level operative parameters, so a directionally specific alternative can score high on X and only mid on Y.
Correcting an error in what the proposal says differs from identifying what it fails to say or commit to.
Both score a step-by-step chain through behavior and implementation to the claimed consequence.
X also covers ambiguous or circular definitions where no two sub-cases are being wrongly merged, which is all Y credits.
Whether the substance is inside the comment text is unrelated to whether it contains integrated quantitative evidence.
Both score named groups bearing differential risks or benefits with the mechanism specified.
X keys on preserving the proposal's objective, Y on filling in draftable operative parameters; a parameterless but well-justified alternative splits them.
Proposing monitoring machinery is unrelated to pinpointing rule text and specifying a revision.
Self-containment of the comment's substance is unrelated to the rigor of any legal argument it contains.
Both score operational-level detail on actors, workflows, and systems that determines whether the rule can actually be executed.
Y additionally requires the experience be used as evidence about a specific regulatory mechanism, not merely reported.
Both score whether the comment situates the proposal against other rules and reasons about conflict or coordination versus treating it in isolation.
Quantified baseline comparison is unrelated to tracing second-order effects across connected systems.
Both require handling the agency's own stated basis — its reasoning, figures, or cited studies — rather than arguing on general grounds.
An exact requested change can be specified without identifying the proposed provision it targets, which Y requires.
X requires an explicit decision consequence drawn from a record-absent fact, while Y requires citation to a specific provision or legal standard.
Both score which groups bear distinct costs or benefits and the concrete exposure mechanism, zeroing out generic public-interest language.
Pinpointing and explaining provisions is unrelated to supplying provision-linked numeric figures.
X is confined to procedural asks with a record-grounded reason; Y covers any precise substantive request and has no procedural requirement.
Cross-rule conflict analysis is unrelated to proposing indicators and verification methods.
A flawed definition already in the text is distinct from a commitment or decision the proposal never makes.
Both require specific numbers that actively carry the argument about the rule rather than appearing as decoration.
X accepts any strongest contrary rationale including another commenter's or an obvious objection, while Y requires countering the agency's own NPRM reasoning.
Both enumerate the same elements — responsible actors, required systems and resources, workflows and timing — that determine practical workability.
Both score a step-by-step causal mechanism from the requirement to the claimed consequence versus bare assertion.
Y additionally requires the personal account be tied to a specific provision or legal standard, which a described personal stake need not be.
X requires diagnosing a structural design flaw as well as offering the alternative; Y requires only the workable alternative that preserves the objective.
Both score an explicit link-by-link causal chain connecting the rule to its claimed consequence.
Both score whether a concrete, implementable substitute design is offered rather than mere objection.
Both separate comments that engage identified proposed provisions from those offering only generic support or sentiment, with near-identical zero anchors.
Explaining how provisions operate is different from alleging a specific error, ambiguity, or misstatement in the quoted wording.
Both score depth of on-the-ground operational knowledge used to expose realities the rule fails to account for.
